articles.title_orig: Seoul must not be sidelined at the U.S.-China-Russia summit
articles.title_zh: Seoul must not be sidelined at the U.S.-China-Russia summit
articles.content_orig:
South Korea must ensure that its security and North Korean denuclearization are not traded away at the upcoming U.S.-China-Russia summit.
The first summit involving the leaders of the United States, China and Russia is scheduled for Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, or APEC, summit in Shenzhen, China. The gathering of U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, representing three nuclear powers, will inevitably attract international attention. But concerns outweigh expectations that the meeting could revive the nightmare of the 1945 Yalta Conference, when major powers reshaped the international order without consulting the countries directly affected.
The three leaders approach the meeting with different calculations. Trump, weakened by his party’s midterm election defeat, hopes to secure diplomatic achievements through nuclear arms reduction and a resolution of the Iran war; Putin stands to benefit simply by escaping diplomatic isolation over Russia’s invasion of Ukraine; and Xi seeks diplomatic leadership but remains reluctant to discuss nuclear disarmament because of China’s comparatively smaller arsenal.
Their conflicting interests make agreement difficult. Nevertheless, transactional diplomacy involving concessions among major powers remains possible, with potentially profound consequences for security on the Korean Peninsula.
The greatest concern is that South Korea could be excluded from discussions about its own security while the North’s status as a nuclear weapons state gains tacit acceptance.
With the White House leaving open the possibility of Trump meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, Pyongyang is also moving quickly. Following his recent visit to Dandong, Kim dispatched Kim Song-nam, the Workers’ Party’s international affairs secretary, to China and close aide Jo Yong-won to Russia.
By strengthening ties with Beijing and Moscow, Pyongyang may seek relief from international sanctions and abandonment of the denuclearization objective.
After World War II, smaller nations, including South Korea, became objects of negotiation rather than participants determining their own destinies. That history explains why Kyiv fears another Yalta and why Tokyo worries about closer cooperation among Washington, Beijing and Moscow.
South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun was therefore right to warn the United States and China against discussing Korean Peninsula affairs unilaterally.
The government must mobilize every diplomatic channel, strengthen South Korea-U.S. coordination and trilateral cooperation with Japan and maintain communication with China and Russia. Preserving the principle of North Korean denuclearization must remain paramount.
Above all, Seoul must secure a firm commitment from Washington that any negotiations with Pyongyang will not replace denuclearization with a nuclear freeze or arms control arrangement.
The South cannot afford to become a bargaining chip in negotiations among nuclear powers. It must directly represent and protect its security interests throughout the diplomatic process.
Seoul should focus its diplomatic resources on ensuring that the Shenzhen summit strengthens regional peace, not repeat the Yalta experience of 81 years ago, when its future was determined by decisions made elsewhere.

articles.title_orig: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
articles.title_zh: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
articles.content_orig:
The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishment
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the  company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.
Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".
The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?
Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".
China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

articles.title_orig: Trump to meet with Xi, Putin at APEC summit in China
articles.title_zh: Trump to meet with Xi, Putin at APEC summit in China
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .

SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_zh: Putin's war machine tied to troubling recruitment of young women as new deals emerge
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian investigator Solomiya Khoma tells Fox News Digital how alleged recruiters and Russian cultural groups draw young African women into Russia’s military-industrial workforce as new agreements with African governments raise concerns.
Two African governments have signed new agreements with a Russian industrial complex linked to the production of attack drones used against Ukraine, even as a Ukrainian investigation alleges Moscow is expanding a recruitment network that draws young African women into its military-industrial workforce.
The agreements, signed in late October by Ghana and the Democratic Republic of the Congo with Russia's Alabuga Special Economic Zone, come months after Britain sanctioned individuals and entities associated with the Alabuga Start program over deceptive recruitment practices. The new partnerships raise questions about whether Russia's efforts to attract foreign workers could help sustain drone production as its war against Ukraine continues.
The Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre says it has obtained internal documents identifying approximately 50 African women employed at Alabuga, alongside 10 Russian recruiters and two African intermediaries allegedly involved in attracting foreign workers.
OUR ADVERSARIES ARE EVEN USING THE US BANKING SYSTEM. HERE’S HOW THEY GET AWAY WITH IT
The remains of a Russian-made, Iran-designed Shahed-136 drone, known in Russia as a Geran-2, are displayed with other recovered drones, glide bombs, missiles and rockets in Kharkiv on July 30, 2025. (Scott Peterson/Getty Images)
"What we were able to do is basically to obtain internal documentation," Solomiya Khoma, the organization's head of international cooperation, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.
Khoma said the investigation went beyond previous reporting by attempting to establish how recruitment operates across borders, connecting Russian cultural organizations, local intermediaries and Alabuga's human resources department. "Our case is specifically related to African countries," she said.
According to the report, the alleged network operates on three levels: Russian cultural and educational organizations cultivating relationships with young people in Africa, local recruiters promoting opportunities abroad, and Alabuga personnel arranging employment and logistics.
A satellite image shows possible planned location of UAV manufacturing plant in Russia's Alabuga Special Economic Zone, as evidence of new Russian-Iran cooperation, in this handout acquired June 9, 2023. (White House/Handout via Reuters)
The investigation identifies two women from Tunisia and Uganda as alleged recruitment coordinators and describes connections with Russian HR personnel and foreign employees. Their specific recruitment activities have not been independently verified by Fox News Digital.
Khoma said the findings relied partly on a confidential source who remains employed within the Alabuga industrial complex.
"This person is still continuing to work in the Alabuga economical zone and these factories," she said, explaining why the organization could not disclose the source's identity.
She said investigators obtained information about the workers and their identities, including internal employee passes.
The researchers also examined the involvement of Russian cultural organizations, including councils of Russian compatriots and the Russkiy Mir Foundation, in promoting educational and employment opportunities in African countries.
The report points to a September 2024 cooperation memorandum between the Russian compatriots' council in Tunisia and Alabuga, alongside Russian cultural activities in Uganda. However, the investigation does not establish that Russian diplomats or cultural organizations knowingly directed recruits into military drone production.
The findings build on an Associated Press investigation published in October 2024 , which documented how African women recruited with promises of education and civilian employment were assigned to manufacture Iranian-designed attack drones . Some described long hours, lower-than-promised wages, surveillance and exposure to hazardous chemicals.
Russia's President Vladimir Putin and the Democratic Republic of the Congo's President Felix Tshisekedi arrive for their meeting on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa Summit at the Grand Kremlin Palace in Moscow, Russia, October 30, 2026. (Pavel Bednyakov/Pool via Reuters)
Khoma described a recruitment process in which women arrive in Russia expecting to combine education with paid employment, only to fail entrance examinations or Russian-language requirements.
"These people are promised a dual education opportunity," she said.
After failing examinations, she alleged, workers may find themselves with limited options and unable to afford transportation home, leaving them performing factory work instead of pursuing their expected studies.
The recruitment program has also attracted international scrutiny. On May 5, 2026, the British government sanctioned seven individuals and entities associated with Alabuga Start recruitment, accusing the operation of using deceptive practices to obtain foreign labor for facilities producing military drones.
Yet cooperation with African governments appears to be continuing.

Ghanaian broadcaster Citi News reported October 29 that Labor Minister Emmanuel Agyekum signed an agreement with Alabuga to facilitate industrial employment opportunities for Ghanaian citizens. The ministry said it would coordinate recruitment, verify job offers and provide pre-departure orientation.
Meanwhile, CongoRassure reported October 30 that the Democratic Republic of the Congo signed a five-year memorandum focused on vocational training and strengthening employment institutions.
Russia's President Vladimir Putin and Ghana's President John Dramani Mahama enter a hall before the beginning of their talks on the sidelines of the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, Russia, October 30, 2026. (Anastasia Barashkova/Pool/Reuters)
Neither agreement, as publicly described, establishes that either government intended to supply workers for military production.
Khoma called for sanctions targeting the recruitment networks themselves, including intermediaries, financial channels and organizations facilitating foreign labor recruitment.
She argued that Russia's efforts to attract workers from abroad reflect growing labor shortages across its wartime economy and represent another potential point of international pressure.

articles.title_orig: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
articles.title_zh: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
articles.content_orig:
A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.
Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.
The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.
Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.
"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."
When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.
He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.
"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.
The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.
The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".
Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.
The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.
Han said he had only cheated to try and earn money and get a job that would make his parents proud of him again.
Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency told Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday that it was looking into the case.
"We received a written confession through the test taker's lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam," it confirmed in a statement.
It added that the case had now been assigned to investigators.
Because of the significance of the national exams, instances of cheating are not uncommon in South Korea, and cases involving the use of AI have become more prominent as the technology becomes more sophisticated.
Last month, two college applicants were reported to have used AI glasses to try and cheat their entrance exams at two Seoul universities.
Education ministry data also says there were four cases of cheating through AI glasses at middle and high schools in the past 12 months.

articles.title_orig: Yemeni government force retreats from strait in major setback in war against Houthis
articles.title_zh: Yemeni government force retreats from strait in major setback in war against Houthis
articles.content_orig:
Yemeni forces fighting for the internationally recognised Saudi-backed government said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, leaving the Iran-aligned Houthis in control.
The government’s retreat ​from the Bab el Mandeb area hands the Houthis greater leverage over the maritime chokepoint, creating ‌a potent pressure point on global shipping while Iran continues to disrupt traffic through the Strait of Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.
This dual squeeze would further isolate Gulf oil producers from their main shipping routes.
The Bab el Mandeb Strait is one ​of the world’s most important and busiest routes for global seaborne commodity and goods shipments, particularly ​from Asia to Europe via Egypt’s Suez Canal.
The southern Yemeni forces said they were ⁠redeploying toward Aden, where the government is based, as the Houthis — who control much of the north, ​including the capital Sanaa and Yemen’s most populous areas — increase pressure on the southern areas still under government control.
“The Southern ​Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the southern forces said in a statement.
“This step is taken based on the priority of securing the ​capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats.”
Government ​forces launched a military campaign in October to recapture the strategic coastal areas from the powerful militia, which had pushed south ‌in September ⁠in an attempt to seize control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast. The lightning offensive brought the Houthis within reach of Bab el Mandeb.
The escalation in fighting, which broke a 2022 UN-brokered truce, became another volatile front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran, as the Houthis continue to launch attacks on Saudi Arabia, a key US ​ally and the world’s biggest ​crude exporter.
Houthi attacks on ⁠the kingdom, which had enjoyed relative calm during the early months of the nine-month-old Iran war, have disrupted flights and oil supplies as the Houthis struck Saudi ​ports, airports and facilities of state oil company Saudi Aramco — including the kingdom’s Red Sea oil ​export hub ⁠of Yanbu.
In response, Saudi Arabia struck Houthi targets in Yemen, a country mired in civil war since 2014, when the Houthis pushed the government south. Impoverished Yemen has been grappling with one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
Fighting ⁠is intensifying ​around the western region of Taiz, with humanitarian conditions worsening. The ​city, which hosts about half of the 300,000 people displaced across Yemen by the latest fighting, remains besieged. Aid supplies are unable to ​enter, and civilians are unable to leave.

articles.title_orig: Romania slams ‘unacceptable’ drone strikes on Black Sea ships
articles.title_zh: Romania slams ‘unacceptable’ drone strikes on Black Sea ships
articles.content_orig:
Romanian Prime Minister Luca Niculescu on Sunday condemned drone strikes on three commercial ships near his country's Black Sea coast, promising to work with NATO allies to strengthen security in the region following the latest attacks.
“These incidents are unacceptable and constitute a violation of international law,” Niculescu said in a post on X. He added that Russia's war against Ukraine was causing the security situation in the Black Sea to deteriorate.
The ships were hit Saturday evening and overnight near Sulina, a Romanian port where the Danube River meets the Black Sea.
The Greek-flagged oil tanker Evia Petrol V was struck just after 9 p.m., followed 35 minutes later by a strike on another ship, the Marsol, according to a statement from Romania's defense ministry published on its Facebook page.
“In both cases, the fires were extinguished by the ships' crews. No casualties were reported,” the ministry said.
A third vessel, the Ali Najafov, also reported being struck overnight. It remains unclear who launched the drones.
Romania's military detected aerial targets on radar and sent F-16 fighter jets into the air. Authorities also issued warnings to residents near the coast about possible drone threats.
The attacks came after another commercial ship, the Larissa 1, was reportedly hit by a drone near Romania's coast on Friday.
Romanian Defense Minister Ștefan-Radu Oprea said Sunday he would raise the incidents with allied counterparts in Brussels. “We need the solidarity of our allies,” he said, calling for more surveillance aircraft and equipment to defend against drones.
Last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the EU will help finance some Black Sea security costs following recent attacks on commercial shipping.
In October, at least seven commercial vessels were struck by drones in the Black Sea close to NATO and EU members Romania and Bulgaria, leaving more than 20 sailors dead and dozens missing.

articles.title_orig: FDA rejects Summit’s ivonescimab, derailing US arrival of much-hyped PD-1xVEGF class
articles.title_zh: FDA rejects Summit’s ivonescimab, derailing US arrival of much-hyped PD-1xVEGF class
articles.content_orig:
The immuno-oncology revolution will have to wait.
The FDA has issued a complete response letter to Summit Therapeutics, declining to approve the highly anticipated PD-1xVEGF bispecific ivonescimab for patients with previously treated, EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer.
The rejection derails the immediate U.S. launch of a drug class that many industry heavyweights believe could eventually dethrone Merck & Co.’s Keytruda.
Summit’s initial application targeted a niche, and as Leerink Partners analysts pointed out in a Nov. 5 note, the limitations of the clinical trial behind the application are not directly transferable to Summit’s broader development program for ivonescimab.
To industry watchers, the regulatory snub does not come as a total surprise. In their Nov. 5 note, Leerink analysts assigned Summit’s bid a 40% probability to approval. That’s because the phase 3 Harmoni trial underpinning Summit’s application failed to meet its overall survival (OS) endpoint, even as the FDA specifically demanded a statistically significant death reduction.
At the primary overall survival analysis of the global Harmoni trial last year, the OS hazard ratio was 0.98 in the Western subgroup, indicating no survival benefit for ivonescimab plus chemotherapy versus chemo alone at that time. Summit argued that the OS data in the Western cohort was too immature compared to the China cohort, and subsequent data cuts showed that Western results improved to 0.76 by June 2026, matching the result from the entire trial. The FDA, however, apparently decided to stick with its OS requirement.
In the CRL, the FDA noted that, without a statistically significant OS improvement, Summit has not established substantial evidence of effectiveness, and that a progression-free survival (PFS) benefit in the absence of a statistically significant OS does not support a positive benefit-risk profile in support of approval, according to Summit.
“We are disappointed for patients and their families awaiting additional treatment options in this setting,” Robert Duggan, chairman and co-CEO of Summit said in a Nov. 15 release.
Before FDA handed out the rejection, Summit had parted ways with its chief commercial officer Robert LaCaze and several senior commercial and marketing leaders who were tasked with building ivonescimab’s launch plan.
Meanwhile, back in China, where ivonescimab’s original developer, Akeso, is in charge, authorities granted the drug its first approval in May 2024 in the same indication of tyrosine kinase inhibitor-pretreated EGFR-mutated nonsquamous NSCLC. Then, the China-only Harmoni-A trial, part of which was merged into the global Harmoni trial, met its OS endpoint at the final analysis with a 26% death risk reduction.
Ivonescimab’s setback has narrowed its potential first-mover advantage as several pharma giants— including Merck —race to advance their own PD-(L)1xVEGF bispecifics.
Pfizer’s 3SBio-partnered tivunatamig (PF-08634404), BioNTech and Bristol Myers Squibb’s pumitamig , Merck’s MK-2010 and AbbVie’s ABBV-1480 are all getting pushed into global phase 3 trials.
Even in the second-line EGFR-mutated NSCLC space, ivonescimab’s absence means one less competitor for TROP2-directed antibody-drug conjugates such as AstraZeneca and Daiichi Sankyo’s Datroway and Merck’s Kelun-Biotech-partnered sac-TMT , as well as BMS’ dual-targeting EGFRxHER3 bispecific ADC, iza-bren .
Now, attention around the PD-(L)1xVEGF class is shifting to the all-important first-line NSCLC setting. As Leerink’s analysts noted, the real test for ivonescimab remains the upcoming readout from the Harmoni-3 trial in first-line NSCLC.
Summit scared investors in April, when a newly added interim analysis of the trial’s squamous cohort missed statistical significance on PFS. The squamous subgroup is now moving toward a final PFS analysis by the end of this year, and the nonsquamous group could report PFS data in the first half of 2027.
Despite the regulatory sting, Summit is far from defeated. Just weeks before the FDA’s decision, the biotech secured a $2 billion cash injection from AZ.
The company now has the financial firepower to fund additional trials for ivonescimab, and AZ plans to pair its sprawling ADC pipeline with the PD-1xVEGF drug, an approach that some considered the next-frontier in immuno-oncology.
“With five positive Phase III studies between Summit and Akeso, nothing changes with respect to our ever-growing belief in the opportunity for ivonescimab and our determination to advance ivonescimab’s development,” Duggan said. “Our mission remains to improve outcomes for patients facing significant unmet needs, which is work worth doing, and we will continue through our expansive clinical development program.”

articles.title_orig: Israel kills a top Hamas commander as Jordan sentences 3 in church attack, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Israel kills a top Hamas commander as Jordan sentences 3 in church attack, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Israel killed a senior Hamas commander involved in planning the October 7 attacks only two months after killing his predecessor, a fresh sign of how the Gaza conflict remains active despite a US-brokered ceasefire being in place.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) killed Samir Mahmoud Abu Younis, the commander of Hamas’ Rafah Brigade, in a strike in southern Gaza overnight Saturday, both Hamas and the IDF said.
Abu Younis, who was a long-time member of the brigade, had replaced Nael Abu Obeid, the previous commander who was killed in a strike in September. And Abu Obeid himself replaced Mohammad Sabaneh, another commander of the Rafah Brigade who was killed in May 2025.
The strike comes just days after an Israeli attack on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, in what the IDF said was an attempt to kill another Hamas commander.
In a statement, Hamas’ military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, acknowledged the death of Abu Younis, saying he had joined the brigade in 1991 and was “among the most prominent commanders who participated in planning and overseeing” the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023.
“The IDF continues to eliminate Hamas leaders in Gaza, and another one joins his predecessors in the depths of hell,” said Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz. “The offensive policy that I am leading together with the Prime Minister and the IDF in Gaza will continue – until Gaza is demilitarized and there is no Hamas.”
The killing of Abu Younis underscores an emerging pattern in Gaza. Despite a nominal ceasefire that went into effect more than one year ago, Israel has continued to carry out strikes targeting members of Hamas, particularly senior commanders. But those commanders are quickly replaced as Hamas entrenches its own grip on power over the half of Gaza not occupied by Israel.
Meanwhile, the Board of Peace, a body created by the Trump administration with United Nations backing to oversee the Gaza ceasefire plan, remains sidelined, unable to make any substantive progress on the 20-point plan agreed to in October 2025.
On Friday, the board said it had held “very constructive discussions” with 17 countries about a civilian Gaza police force under the authority of a Palestinian technocratic committee that was supposed to run Gaza. But that committee has yet to enter the enclave, and an international security force meant to stabilize Gaza has yet to materialize.
The IDF strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza last week killed at least six people, including a doctor and a child, according to Palestinian officials. The strike hit the hospital’s surgery unit, killing Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira and a 13-year-old boy who was awaiting surgery. A total of 40 others were injured in the strike, including two doctors who were in critical condition, officials said.
In a statement, the IDF said it had targeted the commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade, Muhammad Abu Ismail, as well as “additional terrorists who were hiding inside the Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis.” But when pressed on whether Abu Ismail was killed in the strike, the IDF did not answer.
Doctors Without Borders (Médicins Sans Frontières, or MSF) condemned the strike, saying: “It is unconscionable that patients and medical staff are once again being killed and injured inside a hospital, a place where lives should be saved, not taken.” MSF withdrew its own staff from the hospital in January because of the presence of armed men inside, as well as concerns over the hospital’s neutrality and management. “Under international humanitarian law, hospitals must be respected and protected,” MSF said.
The Board of Peace also urged both Israel and Hamas to uphold their commitments under the Comprehensive Peace Plan and protect civilians.
According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, more than 1,600 people have been killed in near-daily Israeli strikes in Gaza since the ceasefire was signed one year ago.
The shattered territory also faces an unfolding humanitarian crisis ahead of the onset of winter. Last week, seasonal rains swamped tens of thousands of tents across Gaza, where nearly two million Palestinians remain displaced.
Israel said that more than 91,000 tents had entered Gaza ahead of winter, but it has refused to allow in the heavy equipment needed for large-scale clean-up and rubble removal efforts.
“The reconstruction of Gaza can only begin after Hamas fully disarms,” said Israel’s Coordinator for Government Activities in the Territories.

articles.title_orig: Chinese electric passenger plane completes first crewed flight
articles.title_zh: Chinese electric passenger plane completes first crewed flight
articles.content_orig:
A Chinese electric passenger plane completed its first crewed flight on Saturday, marking a historic first for China’s aviation industry and the state-backed Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (COMAC), state media reported.
The aircraft was reportedly manned by two pilots and an engineer as it flew for around 60 kilometres, staying airborne for 16 minutes and 38 seconds.
It took off and landed in Binzhou, Shandong Province, in eastern China. China’s state broadcaster CCTV News and the Xinhua news agency first reported on the flight.
The plane, a CE-25A designed for short-distance commercial flights between cities, used an electric propulsion system. It can carry 19 passengers and has a maximum takeoff weight of 10 tonnes. It has a cruising speed of up to 300 km per hour and can fly at an altitude of 2,400 metres.
COMAC said the flight "operated normally." The aircraft was built in China as a collaborative effort between COMAC and battery manufacturer Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL), Shanghai Jiao Tong University and others.
The manned flight is the latest step in the plane's development. It had already flown autonomously in February this year and has since completed 19 unmanned test flights.
The manufacturer applied for type certification from the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC) but has yet to receive approval to enter commercial service.

articles.title_orig: Space data centers could end stargazing as we know it
articles.title_zh: Space data centers could end stargazing as we know it
articles.content_orig:
Illustrative photo. Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
Researchers say governments and companies should wait until the risks of space data centers are better understood and managed before putting them in orbit.
Networks of space data centers could make it nearly impossible for people to stargaze. The report identifies this as one of many risks of placing tens of thousands of AI computers into orbit. Most Americans don’t want data centers built near them, but moving them into space brings a different set of problems.
This is reported by Axios .
The report’s academic researchers urged companies and policymakers to proceed with great caution. It says widespread deployment could make satellites, rather than stars, the most visible points of light in the sky during much of the night across much of the world, echoing astronomers’ concerns.
The report also says that if the U.S. military adopts the technology, data centers could become potential targets in future space conflicts. Thousands of orbital data centers whipping around Earth at 17,000 miles per hour mean a growing risk of collisions and dangerous space debris. And although the centers would run on solar power, the vast number of rocket launches needed to put them in orbit would generate greenhouse gases and black carbon emissions.
Columbia University’s David Sandalow, the report’s lead author, told Axios that there are still “unknown unknowns” about the effects of space data centers.
“If this is going to happen, it should happen slowly and with care,” Sandalow said. “Not just launching lots and lots of these things and, kind of, seeing what happens. ... There's big risks.”
Despite the concerns, investment in orbital data centers is growing. Market research firm Quilty Space says around $197 million in investments were tied to orbital data centers in 2025, rising to $1.11 billion so far in 2026.
According to the Secure World Foundation, SpaceX has applied for a constellation of 1 million data center satellites. Starcloud and Blue Origin’s Project Sunrise have ambitions for 88,000 and 51,600 satellites, respectively.
Caleb Henry, Quilty Space’s director of research, said companies may be filing for more satellites than they are likely to deploy because they do not want to have to raise their proposed numbers later.
“We're at a point where people are tallying paper filings as if they are substantive and real,” Henry said, “and we just don't know that yet.”
The researchers said governments and companies should wait until the risks and impacts of space data centers are better understood and well managed before putting them in orbit.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo helps Argentines embrace Francis, the pontiff who once divided them
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo helps Argentines embrace Francis, the pontiff who once divided them
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV is holding a mass in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba in northern Peru on Saturday as he continues his tour of South America, drawing huge crowds as people seek to catch a glimpse of the 71-year-old pontiff.
After travelling by helicopter from Chiclayo air base to Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, Leo flies back for a prayer meeting with the Catholic community at the shrine of Saint Toribio de Mogrovejo in the evening.
The pope returned to his beloved former hometown of Chiclayo on Friday.
The Chicago-born pontiff, who previously worked as a missionary and then bishop in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship, presided over an open-air mass for around 500,000 people in the city.
"What a joy it is to return to Chiclayo!" Leo said. "Thank you for your affection, support and prayers, especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming."
But the huge crowds turning out to see the pope have prompted heightened fears among health authorities in Latin America, which has seen a surge in measles cases this year.
From January to the end of October, 57,666 confirmed cases were recorded in 17 countries and territories in the Americas, almost five times more than in the same period the previous year. At least 81 deaths have been reported.
Ahead of Leo's visit, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) considered the public health risk of measles "very high" in the context of the expected religious mass gatherings.
The concern is mainly linked to low vaccination rates in some countries, particularly Argentina and Peru.
"We’re seeing children not going to school, children being hospitalized," Daniel Salas Peraza, the head of immunization at PAHO, said. "It’s a very complex situation."
Measles is a highly contagious airborne disease caused by a virus. It can lead to severe complications and is potentially fatal.
The disease infects the respiratory tract and then spreads throughout the body. It can cause symptoms including a high fever, a cough, a runny nose and a rash.
An effective and relatively cheap vaccine is available.
According to the World Health Organisation, "children should receive two doses of the vaccine to ensure they are immune."
"The first dose is usually given at nine months of age in countries where measles is common and 12–15 months in other countries. A second dose should be given later in childhood, usually at 15–18 months," the agency says.
To stop the disease from spreading in a community and to protect infants and others who are unable to get the vaccine, at least 95% of the population must be fully vaccinated.
According to WHO data for 2025, only Uruguay had reached this threshold. In Peru, coverage stood at 90% for the first dose and 82% for the second. In Argentina, the figures fell to 84% and 55% respectively.
Peru has recorded almost 3,000 cases in 2026, the fourth highest number in the Americas after Guatemala, Mexico and the United States.
In the five cities included in the Pope's itinerary - Lima, Chiclayo, Cajamarca, Cusco and Pucallpa - 170 infections have been detected so far this year.
In the run-up to the visit, Peruvian authorities stepped up vaccination campaigns, focusing especially on areas with higher transmission rates.
Initiatives have also included bringing forward vaccination for children between six and eleven months of age and campaigns targeting people up to 29 years old. By the end of September, 1.2 million doses had been administered since the push began in April, while more than two million additional doses were available.
The situation is also tricky in Argentina, where at the end of October, authorities issued a warning about the health risks linked to the Pope's visit. Up to four million people were expected in Buenos Aires province.
Experts are also worried about government cuts to health spending, which have scaled back the structures responsible for planning, funding and monitoring immunisation campaigns.
For its part, Uruguay has launched a period of enhanced epidemiological surveillance across the nation, which will continue until 29 November, weeks after the pope's departure.
Authorities have also intensified appeals to the public to complete their vaccination courses. The aim is to detect any new infections quickly and limit the spread of the virus after the large gatherings.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spot
articles.title_zh: Anthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spot
articles.content_orig:
Between rising interest rates, a nationwide AI backlash, a major political shift in Washington, D.C., and the sudden ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , the tech industry is under mounting strain.
Now comes the most important tech IPO in years, and a defining event for the burgeoning but still young artificial intelligence market.
With Anthropic expected to debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, the stakes are sky-high for almost every major tech company. Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company are collectively investing $26 billion at the IPO price, which is currently expected at $70 to $78 a share. Some of those companies are existing investors, as is early backer Amazon , whose stake could be in the hundreds of billions of dollars.
In addition to all the cash on the line, tech giants also need Anthropic's spending for many years to come. The Claude creator and its top rival, OpenAI, are driving an outsized amount of the AI buildout, and are burning historic amounts of money in the process.
Anthropic has outstanding spending commitments of over $900 billion, according to its latest prospectus . It's on the hook to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon over the course of a decade, and another $400 billion with other companies for cloud capacity, according to filings and partner disclosures. The lab also made $300 billion in commitments with data center and chip partners. Anthropic intends to lay out $125 billion to $150 billion for AI chips from Google , though delivery won't start until 2028.
"The numbers are just staggering," Joe Fath, a partner at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager, said in an interview. "It's hard to get your head wrapped around it."
Cloud partners Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31% of contractual obligations, Anthropic said in its prospectus. Last year, Amazon built an Indiana data center just for Anthropic, using custom chips.
By going public now, Anthropic can raise a large portion of the money it needs to pay for the technology and infrastructure required for building and hosting its frontier models and expanding portfolio of services. The company recorded a net loss of $104 billion through the first nine months of 2026. The IPO could yield over $90 billion in proceeds, on top of Anthropic's $132 billion in existing cash, including short-term investments.
The length of Anthropic's contracts is also unique. Typically such contracts last five years or less, while Anthropic's agreement with Amazon extends for twice that amount of time.
"Realistically, anything past three to four years, you're basically throwing darts in the dark," said Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at spend management software vendor Duckbill. "It is almost a certainty that it will be renegotiated long before the culmination of that contract."
Meanwhile, a data center for Anthropic that starts leasing in 2027 has a 20-year term. For both space and computing, Anthropic is splurging now so it doesn't end up short on capacity long into the future.
"In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment," Anthropic said in the prospectus.
Anthropic and Amazon didn't provide a comment.
It's a tough time for Anthropic to hit the Nasdaq, with the offering coming as tech investors are desperate for some good news. The Nasdaq is down to start November after dropping 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025.
Rising interest rates pushed investors out of debt-heavy neoclouds , which have become a critical piece of the infrastructure buildout. And in the midterm elections earlier this month, Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress and in key gubernatorial races, while dozens of ballot measures were passed that will potentially limit new data center development across the country.
Then came the Nvidia crisis. Shares of the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom tumbled 13% this week to their lowest since July 2025, after Huang's multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, led to his ouster early Thursday. Huang was replaced on an interim basis with CFO Colette Cress , who faces a major test on Tuesday, two days before the Anthropic debut, as Nvidia is set to report quarterly results.
The ongoing Nvidia fallout and the Anthropic IPO create quite the split-screen moment for tech's heavyweights, which are closely tied to both companies.
Google will be paying particularly close attention.
The company is set to own about 13% of Anthropic after the IPO, and is backstopping the lab's $19 billion in lease commitments to Terawulf , which will supply data center space in Kentucky. If Anthropic goes insolvent, Google will step in and pay the remaining rent or a termination fee, Terawulf said .
"Everybody knows that Anthropic is going to be the future of Google," said Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google cloud partnerships leader who now advises companies.
Google didn't provide a comment.
One major impetus for Anthropic to enter costly and long-term guarantees is that OpenAI is being equally aggressive, and capacity is limited, particularly for graphics processing units. Going long can mean locking in rates as the industry confronts questions about whether data center development will slow.
"You will need to be in a rush to get infrastructure, and if you are not going to be there, you will be out of business," said Eli Mansoor, CEO of OskaQ Consulting, which advises companies on cloud negotiations. "It used to be that prices always go down, but this is changing, especially in the GPU world."
Big financial firms are lining up to help Anthropic get what it wants. Bank of America , Blackstone , Citigroup and Morgan Stanley have offered $63 billion to buy racks full of Broadcom AI chips that Anthropic will rent. Broadcom has provided a backstop with a maximum liability of $43 billion .
That's a lot of silicon and a massive bet for a five-year-old company that's never lived through a technology downturn.
"It's not a risk-free prospect, but I would call it smart investing," said David Tollen, founder of Sycamore Legal, where he specializes in IT contracts. "They're investing, in a sense, in themselves. They're putting money into something that if it succeeds, they get a piece of the action."

articles.title_orig: As US credit card debt hits $1.29T, bank algorithms are rejecting debt-free, six-figure earners
articles.title_zh: As US credit card debt hits $1.29T, bank algorithms are rejecting debt-free, six-figure earners
articles.content_orig:
‘The Ramsey Show’ co-host Jade Warshaw and credit repair analyst Micah Smith speak to Fox News Digital about how high-earning, low-debt consumers may face credit card and loan penalization.
Across the country, Americans earning six-figure salaries, carrying no debt and sitting on healthy savings accounts are increasingly hitting an unexpected wall when applying for everyday credit cards or loans: instant denial from automated bank algorithms.
The rejections highlight a growing rift between kitchen-table financial discipline and corporate underwriting models. While nationwide credit card balances have climbed to a record $1.29 trillion — a 67% surge since early 2021, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York — data from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) shows an estimated 25 million adults have credit files "too thin" or stale to generate a standard score.
Rather than rewarding households that avoid borrowing, modern underwriting algorithms can interpret limited recent credit activity as a sign of uncertain lending risk, potentially making it harder for some debt-free consumers to qualify for credit.
"Is corporate America penalizing people who live debt-free? I would say they're not penalizing them, but they are not prioritizing them because we're not the ones making them money," Jade Warshaw, co-host of "The Ramsey Show" — who paid off $460,000 in debt alongside her husband — told Fox News Digital. "When you think about the credit score in general, the whole purpose, it's a product, and so it's out there for banks to make money. And if we're not going to be their customer, then yes, they're not going to prioritize us."
IRS ANNOUNCES 2027 TAX CHANGES: WHAT TAXPAYERS NEED TO KNOW
"Responsible, debt-free living, while it is something that we as consumers should absolutely strive for, the interesting thing about how credit works is it's very counterintuitive," credit repair specialist and Micah Abigail LLC founder Micah Smith also told Fox News Digital.
While U.S. credit card balances hit a new high, an estimated 25 million Americans have credit files considered "too thin." (Getty Images)
Smith recalled walking into a dealership as a young, debt-free adult to buy her first car, only to be told she was denied financing and needed a co-signer because lenders "couldn't see who she was on paper."
"The algorithms are looking for movement," Smith explained. "They want to see what you've actually been doing. So the interesting thing about credit is that income is never a factor into the score itself. And so you might have this incredible income, but you might not have a credit score that supports exactly who you are as a person."
A 2025 consumer study by PYMNTS Intelligence and the Federal Reserve found that credit anxiety and unexpected loan denials are no longer just low-income struggles, but they increasingly strike households earning over $100,000 due to a lack of borrowing diversity and thin credit files.
Such credit challenges can complicate applications for entry-level credit cards with major providers like Chase or Capital One, as well as financing for cars and mortgages.
Credit card debt hits a record $1.29 trillion as President Donald Trump pushes for a 10% interest rate cap, sparking rare agreement between the left and right.
Warshaw noted that Fair, Isaac and Company, the predecessor of FICO, was founded in 1956 by Bill Fair and Earl Isaac to develop credit risk analytics, not to measure personal wealth, and argued that decades of financial marketing have conditioned Americans to confuse the two.
"As American consumers, we've allowed the credit score to confuse being profitable for banks with us being actually financially good with money, and it's not the same thing," Warshaw said. "Being profitable with banks by having a good credit score does not equal being a financially responsible adult and actually having wealth and being good with money."
Smith also cautioned against "buy now, pay later" platforms as some of them have started reporting to credit bureaus. So, instead of helping with retail purchases, she warns, opening multiple short-term installment loans creates a flurry of new accounts that continuously drags down the "average age of credit" and makes a file look erratic.
"… if you owe money to anyone for any reason, that person has power over you."
"Every time you open something, it’s going to take your overall length of history backwards," Smith said. "It’s opened up as an installment loan — you open it, pay it off and it closes. So having those opened up often could suppress your scores pretty substantially."
The philosophy popularized by Dave Ramsey is that the credit score is simply an "I love debt" score that measures your relationship with lenders as opposed to true financial success. Warshaw advises consumers to cut up their cards and practice total abstinence, warning that credit cards can act as a "gateway drug" that leaves families vulnerable to financial disaster.
"If you look at all the research and data out there, you will find the research that says if you hold credit cards, you are also more likely to hold other forms of consumer debt —  so personal loans, car loans, mortgage debt, all of those things. So credit cards, in that way, it kind of is a gateway drug into the other forms of debt," Warshaw said.
Credit repair influencer and Micah Abigail LLC founder Micah Smith speaks to Fox News Digital about how to make improvements to credit scores in just 30 days, while cautioning against credit misconceptions.
"It's so easy to get behind," she continued. "And I remind people all the time, I say, 'I get it.’ Most people out there who talk to me about credit cards, they say, 'Jade, don't worry, I pay it off every single month.' And I say, 'Really, you pay it off every single month? America has $1.3 trillion in debt. That means someone's lying.'"
Smith agreed that living debt-free is an admirable goal, but argued that voluntarily becoming "invisible" in a digital economy creates expensive, everyday roadblocks when dealing with landlords and co-ops, or operating a small business. She argued, "You will not be able to run a business on cash alone. It doesn't exist."
The credit repair expert recounted a recent trip to Las Vegas where more than $9,000 in travel expenses were funded entirely through accumulated credit card points and cash back rewards.
"I think the Ramsey solution is great for people who don't have the ability to say ‘no.’ If you live responsibly, you need to have credit," Smith said. "You need to have it established because it's going to open doors that cash just won't, and that's just a fact."
The experts offer differing advice for fiscally responsible consumers: keep revolving cards open with low balances to pay off every month, or treat debt as surrendering control and build a 3-to-6-month cash emergency fund.

"The biggest thing that people don't realize is that [with] credit cards, you can have an 800 credit score with just having credit cards, and you want to maintain them. And so open them, use a small amount, pay them off," Smith said. "In the world of FICO, they actually reward tiny little balances, so leave a balance of $1 to $5. That's all you need to ensure it calculates into the credit score."
"Around here, we believe that the borrower is slave to the lender — meaning if you owe money to anyone for any reason, that person has power over you," Warshaw argued. "Credit cards aren't there to build wealth. Credit cards are there as a product to help you overspend and make banks money. But if you really want to be wealthy, son or daughter, what you're going to do is you're going to avoid debt. You're going to take your margin, and you're going to invest it for the future."

articles.title_orig: CEO SUNDAY: BlackBerry boss on the company's evolution from smartphone giant to software powerhouse
articles.title_zh: CEO SUNDAY: BlackBerry boss on the company's evolution from smartphone giant to software powerhouse
articles.content_orig:
BlackBerry CEO John Giamatteo discusses the company’s evolution beyond smartphones and its growing focus on automotive software and secure communications.
For many people, BlackBerry still brings to mind the signature smartphone that was once a staple of corporate America.
But the BlackBerry that CEO John Giamatteo leads today looks very different.
The devices that made the brand a household name are gone. In their place is a software business whose technology largely operates behind the scenes, powering systems in cars, government communications, robotics and medical equipment while securing communications for governments and other critical organizations.
BUILT FROM SCRATCH: HOW A METEOROLOGIST BUILT A BETTER UMBRELLA
"We're a different company than we were from the device days, but we are powering with our software and services the world around us in a lot of different ways," Giamatteo told FOX Business.
For Giamatteo, continuing the reinvention of the brand has meant following a simple playbook of doing fewer things and doing them well.
"Simplify what you're doing," Giamatteo said.
UTAH RARE EARTHS PROJECT COULD REDUCE DEPENDENCE ON CHINA FOR CRITICAL MINERALS
For Giamatteo, continuing the reinvention of the brand has meant following a simple playbook of doing fewer things and doing them well. (BlackBerry)
" Sometimes companies can get a little bit too complicated, and they're into too many different things," he added. "So narrowing your focus on fewer things that you're going to do really well, I think, makes a big difference."
For BlackBerry, that has meant focusing on its automotive software and secure communications businesses.
BlackBerry's QNX embedded software is now used in more than 275 million vehicles, while 18 of the G20 countries use some form of its secure communications technology.
The transformation is also showing up in its financial results.
BlackBerry reported $163.3 million in revenue for its second quarter of fiscal 2027, up 26% from a year earlier, while adjusted EBITDA jumped 81% to $47 million. QNX revenue climbed 27% to a quarterly record of $80.3 million.
Giamatteo also said he brings a numbers-driven approach to running the company.
"I'm a bit of a numbers guy," he said. "I immerse myself in metrics and [key performance indicators]. I like to have data on everything."
He said he reviews BlackBerry's key performance indicators daily, looking for trends and signs of what's working and what isn't.
"I'm not saying it's right, but it's how I'm wired," Giamatteo said. "And it allows me to kind of immerse myself in the business in a number of different ways."

Giamatteo grew up on Long Island and attended St. John's University in Queens. He began his career in finance before going on to hold leadership roles at several technology companies, including more than six years at McAfee.
His career also took him overseas, with two years in Hong Kong and four years in Tokyo, an experience he described as an "inflection point" in his career.
"It kind of made me a little more curious, a little bit more intellectually interested in some of these different markets and cultures and what it means," Giamatteo said.
The experience also reinforced a piece of career advice that has stayed with him.
"Don't be afraid to step out of your comfort zone. That's where you really grow. That's where you really challenge yourself," he said.
Giamatteo said a leadership development program earlier in his career gave him experience across marketing, product, sales and operations, helping him build a broader understanding of how a business operates.
"I really think, at a personal level, that helped me grow and develop in my career," he said, encouraging others to venture beyond their own areas of expertise. "I think you'll be better for it in the long run."

articles.title_zh: The Stock Market Is Doing Something for Only the 6th Time in 156 Years, and History Says It's Clear What Comes Next for Stocks
articles.content_orig:
Despite a few periods of short-lived volatility, 2026 has shaped up as another banner year for the stock market. The ageless Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI +0.10% ) , benchmark S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -0.40% ) , and innovation-powered Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -0.91% ) have reached several record highs, courtesy of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out.
While history decisively shows that Wall Street's major stock indexes rise over long periods, it also tells us that bull markets aren't indefinite and that when things look too good to be true, they typically are .
Currently, we're witnessing the stock market do something for just the sixth time since January 1871 -- and if history has its say, it's pretty clear what comes next for stocks.
Image source: Getty Images.
At any given time, several headwinds are waiting in the wings to knock the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite off their respective pedestals. Current examples include the parabolic increase in outstanding margin debt , persistently elevated inflation, and the potential for an AI bubble-bursting event.
But among this laundry list of headwinds, none stands out more than premium stock valuations.
Given that there's no one-size-fits-all blueprint to evaluate and value individual companies or the broader market, discussing value can be incredibly tricky. The subjectivity and emotion that come into play when valuing stocks or the broader market are what make accurately predicting short-term movements so challenging.
Most investors rely on the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio to quickly evaluate the relative cheapness or priciness of a public company or the broader market. Unfortunately, the traditional P/E ratio isn't perfect. For instance, it loses its utility if corporate earnings turn negative during a recession.
This is where the stock market's most time-tested valuation tool comes in handy: the S&P 500's Shiller P/E Ratio, also known as the Cyclically Adjusted P/E Ratio ( CAPE Ratio ). Since the Shiller P/E Ratio is based on average inflation-adjusted earnings over the trailing 10 years, a recession won't make this valuation tool useless.

When backtested to January 1871, the S&P 500's Shiller P/E Ratio has averaged 17.45. As of the closing bell on Nov. 10, it clocked in at 39.70, or 128% above the long-term average.
While value is a tricky subject to tackle, history has consistently shown that bad things happen when the CAPE Ratio surpasses 30 . The stock market has exceeded this arbitrary line in the sand six times over the last 156 years, including the present, and the previous five all ended poorly for equities:
History makes it abundantly clear that premium valuations lack staying power . Although the Shiller P/E Ratio offers no help in determining when the stock market will top or which catalysts will send stocks over the edge, it has a flawless, 156-year backtested track record of foreshadowing significant downside in the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite.
Image source: Getty Images.
Though history offers a relatively dire outlook for investors, the silver lining is that the outcome can change based on investors' perspectives . While the coming quarters may prove bleak, the long-term outlook for equities has arguably never been brighter.
For example, history shows that stock market corrections and bear markets are inevitable aspects of the investing cycle. No amount of well-wishing can prevent these often emotion-driven double-digit downturns.
But history also shows that stock market corrections and bear markets tend to be short-lived.
In late May, the analysts at independent research firm Bespoke Investment Group published a data set on X (formerly Twitter) that calculated and compared the length of 27 separate S&P 500 bull and bear markets since the start of the Great Depression in September 1929. This data set offered tangible evidence of the milewide gap between optimism and pessimism on Wall Street.
The current bull market that began on 10/12/22 is now the 9th longest in S&P 500 history, surpassing the 1,324-day bull that ended on 2/9/1966: https://t.co/4mGsS2t2ft
According to Bespoke Investment Group, the average S&P 500 bear market has lasted 286 calendar days (about 9.5 months) over the previous 97 years. Furthermore, none of the 27 bear markets surpassed 630 calendar days.
By comparison, the typical S&P 500 bull market has persisted for 1,023 calendar days -- roughly 3.6 times as long as the average S&P 500 bear market -- with 14 of 27 bull markets lasting longer than 630 calendar days.
Although there's no magic predictive tool that can consistently tell us when stock market downturns will begin, history has repeatedly shown that staying the course and buying into substantive dips is a winning strategy for long-term-minded, optimistic investors. Even if history repeats and the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite plunge by at least 20% in the not-too-distant future, patient investors will be well positioned for success.

articles.title_orig: Bugatti's new US CEO talks manuals, electric hypercars and the business of tariffs - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Bugatti's new US CEO talks manuals, electric hypercars and the business of tariffs - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Bugatti recently celebrated 20 years in the U.S.
There's no shortage of hypercars in the world. Brands like Aston Martin, McLaren, Ferrari and Gordon Murray Automotive are building exotic roadsters and coupes that deliver unprecedented power. Then there's Bugatti.
The storied French marque has been producing seven-figure sports cars that are and masterfully engineered and terrifyingly fast for 117 years. Its recent creation, the 1,800-horsepower hybrid Tourbillon, will soon be delivered to discerning clients, a majority of whom are in the U.S.
Sascha Doering, Bugatti's newly appointed CEO of the Americas, understands the importance of selling cars here. It's the top market for the niche automaker and this year the brand is celebrating 20 years in the country, with the Veyron being the first Bugatti to hit U.S. streets.
Seeing a Bugatti in person can be limited to auto shows. Doering may be able to change that -- he's trying to get even more owners to drive their Chirons, Mistrals and Divos more frequently.
"It is, of course, a special experience to take it out," Doering told ABC News.
Bugatti, like all foreign automakers, has not been immune from the tariff pressures. There are also questions on whether Bugatti will stay true to its heritage after it merged with Croatian electric startup Rimac. Doering sat down with ABC News to discuss the brand's long history, how he's keeping customers happy and whether we'll see an electric Bugatti one day.
The interview below has been edited for clarity.
Q: The brand is celebrating 20 years in the U.S. What's your prediction for the next 20 years? Will people be driving cars then?
A: People will be driving our cars, I can tell you that. North America is the single most important market for Bugatti in the world. It's really about creating a community. We have amazing cars. We're just about to deliver Tourbillon. We see this trajectory in the strength of the market continuing. We have incredibly strong customer relationships and bonds.
We know there won't be a self-driving Bugatti in 20 years. Why? Because of emotions. This is an emotional product. The Tourbillon, at its core, has a naturally aspirated, high-revving V16 engine. It's all about goosebumps and emotion. The interior is mechanical and analog. We want our clients to be the happiest kids with their masterpieces. We want our customers to drive [their cars] in 20 years and still have a smile in their eyes. That's why we exist.
Q: The Tourbillon is really an engineering feat. How does the brand surpass that engineering accomplishment?
A: We believe in Mate [Bugatti Rimac CEO]. From an engineering perspective, we believe in our vision of creating the pinnacle of innovation, craftsmanship, luxury and design. This is the only task that we have -- staying true to those principles that honestly we have never diverted on ever in our history. We will continue to push the boundaries, continue to always innovate and set new pinnacles of beauty.
The Destrier is a beautiful masterpiece. It's a different design. It's based on the most extreme chassis that we have (the Bolide). We are fully confident from a design and engineering perspective that there's always another pinnacle to reach.
Q: Let's talk about electrification. The Tourbillon is technically a hybrid. How important is electrification to Bugatti?
A: It's about emotions at the end of the day. And electrification adds an important piece to it. The Tourbillon is truly the best of both worlds: the feel, the sensation, the sound, the vibration of the engine. But it's also a combination of the torque that you have from the electric powertrain.
Q: Bugatti has delivered 353 cars over 20 years to U.S. customers. That's about 17 cars a year. Are you trying to increase that number?
A: We started about 20 years ago in the North America market with a global share of roughly 20%-25%. Now it's 35%-45%. We have been increasing the allocations in the North American market. Customers are really happy with us here. They are seeking the brand and the product.
Last year we delivered around 60 cars for the North American market, an absolute record.
We currently have 12 Bugatti dealerships in the U.S., two in Canada and one in Mexico. There is no need to have more partners. We are not looking to increase capacity output to build more cars.
Q: What are your plans for the brand since taking over as head of the Americas? Are you trying to bring in a younger clientele? New customers?
A: The No. 1 objective for us is to build a strong client community. What I mean is relationships and experiences. We have a strong customer base here in the U.S. and it's important that we spend time with them. A lot of the clients own more than one Bugatti. One client in North America owns 14 Bugattis.
We are in the business of relationships. This is not a transaction. It's actually deeper than that. The journey is a long one. You order a Tourbillon now and we'll spec it with our designers. In four years the car will be delivered.
We see more and more younger buyers interested in the brand. We went from an average [customer] age of 52 to about 42. Our demographics are getting slightly younger.
Q: Is the brand trying to reduce the long wait periods for customer deliveries? Have you heard from unhappy customers?
A: Our customers are very eager to have their cars. We sold the Tourbillon coupe two years ago. We're just about to deliver the first ones in the world. We are targeting global deliveries in Q2 of 2027. In the U.S., we are a few months later than that. That puts us at three-ish years [for deliveries]. The number of cars we produce a year won't change. Currently it's about a 100 cars a year. Residual value is incredibly important to our customers. There will always be a waiting time.
Q: Mate Rimac has said in recent interviews that Bugatti could produce a supercar with a manual transmission. Is that what Bugatti customers are asking for? How likely would this happen?
A: Looking at the general industry, we're going back to the simple basics of things like the emotions of a naturally aspirated engine and manual transmissions. Bugatti will always do its own interpretation of innovation [and] be the most emotional product it can be. And the rest is up to Mate.
Q: Has anyone said to you, Sascha please make an all-electric Bugatti?
Q: What is Bugatti's biggest challenge right now?
A: Bugatti is super strong at the moment. Last year we had tariffs. We delivered all the Mistrals, all of Bolides against the headwind of tariffs. That was a challenge. Why? Because clients were obviously not happy about [the tariffs]. And we helped and supported them. Not one client canceled an order. Are tariffs still here? Yes. Are the tariffs a lot for a $4.6 million Tourbillon? Yes. We have not modified our prices at all. However, the tariffs are getting added on top, which increases the financial burden for the client.
Bugattis, and the final assembly of the Tourbillon, will continue to be built in Molsheim [France].
