articles.title_orig: Strange 'Metal Potatoes' Contain a Microcosm of Life Not Seen Anywhere Else on The Seafloor, Scientists Find
articles.title_zh: Strange 'Metal Potatoes' Contain a Microcosm of Life Not Seen Anywhere Else on The Seafloor, Scientists Find
articles.content_orig:
Polymetallic nodules stud the seafloor throughout the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, and new research shows that each of these strange metal potatoes contains an entire community of microscopic life unique to this habitat.
There's a reason humans have named them polymetallic nodules: we're really interested in the metal part.
Our society's reliance on metals like nickel, cobalt, and copper is growing rapidly, and these nodules are loaded with them, as well as iron and manganese.
But polymetallic nodules are not a readily renewable resource. Though it only takes minutes to pluck a nodule from the seafloor, it took millions of years for it to form.
Scientists are concerned this speculative industry could destroy a unique ecosystem we barely knew existed, before we get a chance to understand it.
"Our findings point out that commercial mining may result in an irreversible loss of undescribed and unique biodiversity associated to nodules," says deep-sea biologist Sabine Gollner, of the Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research.
"This needs to be considered in environmental management of deep-sea mining."
The research is published in Scientific Reports .
The nodules were collected in 2019 by a crew of scientists taking part in an expedition to the Clarion-Clipperton Zone aboard the German research vessel RV Sonne, as part of the JPI Oceans Mining Impact II project.
The team carefully lowered a box corer to depths of around 4 to 6 kilometers (2.5 to 3.7 miles) to take a chunk of seafloor sediment and the nodules embedded within.
For this study, the researchers examined 244 individual nodules looking for signs of life in the cracks and pores.
The nodules – and their marine inhabitants – were then frozen and taken to a lab.
One hundred fifty-three of the nodules came from an area where Germany's Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources (BGR) holds an exploration contract from the International Seabed Authority. A further 91 were collected from an area where Belgian company Global Sea Mineral Resources – a subsidiary of DEME – holds an exploration contract.
Most assessments of biodiversity in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone so far have focused on organisms living in the sediment, or clinging to the nodules' surface.
Much of the deep sea is covered in a fine mud, but many of the animals that live there need a more solid surface to attach to: the polymetallic nodules provide an ideal substrate for those creatures.
"We already knew that polymetallic nodules provide attachment surfaces for deep-sea organisms, but very little was known about the animals living inside them," marine genomicist Coral Diaz-Recio Lorenzo told ScienceAlert.
On cracking the nodules open, scientists found bustling ecosystems in miniature throughout the nooks and crannies.
Roundworms and crustaceans were the most common inhabitants, and one species of ' armored amoeba ', Thurammina , dominated its kind. In just a few nodules, they recorded bristleworms, mud dragons, tardigrades, and other less common critters.
"What surprised us most was how different the communities living inside nodules were from those in nearby sediments," Diaz-Recio Lorenzo said.
"Remarkably, nodule communities collected from areas separated by approximately 1,000 kilometers were more similar to one another than to the surrounding sediment communities."
Using microscopes to look more closely at the nodules, the researchers also found the fossils of diatoms , radiolarians , and sea sponges embedded within the ancient layers.
"The presence of… biogenic particles within crevices indicated that at least some cavity structures were colonized by ancient organisms, although this does not necessarily demonstrate in-situ colonization at the time of incorporation," the team writes .
"Sponge spicules were visible in the [scanning electron microscope] images, and the presence of the Foraminifera species Saccorhiza sp. , which uses sponge spicules to build its tests [shell-like structures], indicates that nodules may have provided a habitat on the seabed for millions of years."
If the ISA grants approval for deep-sea mining companies to take the nodules en masse, these ancient ecosystems will be irreversibly destroyed.
"Because their communities differ from those in the surrounding sediments, protecting sediment habitats alone would not preserve this biodiversity," Diaz-Recio Lorenzo added.
"Large-scale nodule removal could therefore result in irreversible losses of unique species and ecological communities that we are only beginning to understand."
These distant and microscopic worlds may seem quite isolated from ours, but the reality is we have no idea yet how they play into global networks of nutrients, carbon, and ecology.
Scientists are in a race to figure that out, before it's too late.
The research has been published in Scientific Reports .

articles.content_orig:
The largest technology stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade could stand to benefit the most from Nvidia's woes and a Democratic-controlled Congress pushing back on data centers, according to investing experts interviewed on CNBC's " ETF Edge " earlier this week.
"We may have been put in an environment, as much as investors have sort of been looking for areas outside of Big Tech, where net-net Big Tech ends up as the winner once again," said Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza, whose firm manages the Magnificent Seven ETF ( MAGS ).
Part of his bull case: Other players in the AI trade are positioned to fill Nvidia's chip demand if investors lose trust in the company after a tumultuous week that saw its iconic founder and CEO Jensen Huang resign.
"If we get into an environment where people can't trust … Nvidia, they're going to look for other sources for these chips because they need them," Mazza said during the "ETF Edge" interview, which occurred Monday as the Nvidia scandal grew but before Huang had resigned.
Discussing recent fund flow activity for the MAGS ETF, as well as for the Roundhill Neocloud ETF ( NCLD ) — which focuses on smaller market cap, specialized cloud computing companies — Mazza said, "In a weird way, [hyperscalers] may continue to benefit from this because they have the compute available. It's going to be more valuable if the demand is there."
The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF ended the week in the green, albeit with a gain of less than 1%, while the Roundhill Neocloud ETF was up over 1%, though earnings from top holdings Coreweave and Nebius presented a mixed picture.
CoreWeave had its best day since April 2025 on Wednesday after its latest quarterly results, while Nebius shares sank after its Thursday report. The neocloud ETF remains deeply in the red since its August 2026 launch, down 39%, amid concerns about balance sheet strength, which could linger given Nvidia's role in financing the AI buildout. CoreWeave shares sank again on Friday, and Nvidia posted its longest losing streak since 2012 after its latest weekly losses.
Nvidia's interim CEO and current chief financial officer Colette Kress will have her first opportunity to reassure the market when Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings next Tuesday. "Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders," Kress said in a statement issued on Thursday morning when the company announced Huang's exit.
Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director Dan Ives said on "ETF Edge" on Monday that the market will remain optimistic about other AI chip players, like AMD and Alphabet, if Nvidia faces prolonged headwinds. Ives helped create the Dan IVES Wedbush AI Revolution ETF ( IVES ) while at Wedbush Securities, where he served as the managing director and global head of technology research before departing Wedbush to form his own firm earlier this year.
AMD finished trading this week up close to 13%, with Broadcom posting similar gains.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq index posted its best week since August as Nvidia's slump reshuffled the AI trade.
Yorkville Ives lowered its price target on Nvidia to $225 from $300 on Thursday after Huang's resignation, but maintained a buy rating on the stock, which finished the week at $162.85 per share.
"Nvidia remains the clear leader in GPU chips for the AI Revolution. They are roughly 2-3 years ahead of the nearest competitor and the demand trajectory the next few years is not changing because Jensen is gone," Ives wrote in a note to investors on Thursday. "The strategic roadmap is already essentially built around the next few family of chips and physical AI with 42k employees driving it. ... Valuation at roughly 10x 28 EPS is way too cheap once Nvidia gets through this storm and emerges on the other side."
The compute that does exist could become even more indispensable against the backdrop of a potential slowdown to the data-center buildout by Congress after the Democratic Party gains of Nov. 3 swept control of Congress, Mazza said.
Ives estimates that the "blue tidal wave" in Congress could mean 10% of planned data centers won't materialize on the low end, and 15%-20% on the high end, but he added that demand still outstrips supply four to one. "The compute is just that much more valuable in the capacity today than it was a week ago. So I could argue just more and more bullish, strong, get stronger," Ives said.
"The game is going to change for Big Tech. It will slow it down. But there's no overbuild, no bubble concerns. And I view that as actually a positive thing," he added.

articles.title_orig: Ground Stop Ripples Into Third Day of Scrapped Flights
articles.title_zh: Ground Stop Ripples Into Third Day of Scrapped Flights
articles.content_orig:
Effects of a nationwide ground stop on air travel Friday evening, which stranded thousands of passengers and caused widespread delays, have rippled through the weekend , as airlines canceled thousands of flights and airports struggled to recover.
The number of flights facing disruption on Sunday was lower than the day before, according to FlightAware , a flight tracking service, but tens of thousands of passengers still faced snarls. FlightAware said that more than 3,000 flights scheduled for Sunday were either delayed or canceled as of 8:30 a.m. Eastern. More than 15,000 were delayed or canceled on Saturday.
The air traffic control system, which faced a faulty upgrade that caused communications failures leading to the ground stop, is expected to be back to normal by Sunday night, said Bryan Bedford, who leads the Federal Aviation Administration. Flight schedules could take several days to return to normal.
Federal officials are still trying to determine who is at fault and have called for congressional funding to prevent similar failures. There is no evidence that the problem was caused by a cyberattack, officials have said.
L3Harris, a contractor managing the F.A.A.’s telecoms network, made a standard upgrade at a remote air traffic location, federal officials said Saturday. L3Harris was conducting a routine task — replacing copper wire with more modern fiber optic cable — that was expected to pose no significant disruption to air traffic, said Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary.
But the switch from copper to fiber overwhelmed the system with levels of data it could not handle, prompting widespread communications failures across air traffic facilities that manage the national air space. Alarmed at the scope of the problems, officials issued a rare nationwide ground stop for hours.

articles.title_orig: Megaspeed rejects claims over supply chain, says Alice Huang no longer with firm
articles.title_zh: Megaspeed rejects claims over supply chain, says Alice Huang no longer with firm
articles.content_orig:
The Singapore-based company at the center of the scandal that brought down Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Sunday that suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang left the company in 2025. It also denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business."
In a statement to CBS News, Megaspeed International said Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, left the company in August 2025 and has no current role. It did not comment on the allegations that Alice Huang is a suspected Chinese spy.
"Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.
Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed and is the woman with whom Jensen Huang was having an affair. She is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security , which China denies. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO last week.
U.S. investigators say Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China.
In the past three years, Megaspeed has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.
Now the company, which began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to the Nvidia chips, is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips into China.
In a statement to CBS News on Sunday, the company said that recent assertions about its business, supply chain and global operations are "not supported by verifiable evidence."
"Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," it said.
President Trump said last week the FBI was investigating the romantic and business ties between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who are not related.
CBS News reported on Friday that Singaporean authorities seized Alice Huang's passport in June 2025 while trying to engage the U.S. government to support their investigation into the suspected smuggling of Nvidia chips to China, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.
The source added that the Singaporean government received no meaningful help from Washington at the time.

Vladimir Putin's secret grandson has been given a new name after an ironic twist put him a little too close to the Russian dictator's arch-enemy.
Leaked records reveal that Putin's closely guarded family added a new member in August 2025, when his daughter Katerina Tikhonova, 40, gave birth to a son, Adrian, according to the independent Russian investigative news outlet Agentstvo .
The arrival came with one rather inconvenient wrinkle for the 74-year-old despot: by convention, his grandson's last name would be none other than "Zelensky."
Adrian's father is ballet dancer Igor Zelensky, 57, who headed the Bavarian State Ballet in Germany until his father-in-law launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Although Igor Zelensky and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky are not related, it appears to be an association Putin was unwilling to entertain after years of unsuccessfully trying to topple the democratically elected Ukrainian leader.
According to leaked civil registry records, Putin's grandson has been registered as Adrian Tikhonov, taking the masculine form of his mother Katerina's surname rather than his father's.
Adrian's birth certificate was issued by Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital, known as the "Kremlin Clinic."
It took unusually long—11 months—after Adrian's birth for him to be registered.
Katerina Tikhonova, the younger of Putin's two acknowledged daughters, is a former acrobatic dancer who now oversees key Russian AI projects and is linked to drone production, an industry that has become a crucial component of her father's war on Ukraine.
Adrian is Tikhonova's second child with Igor Zelensky. The couple had their firstborn daughter Elsa in 2017.
At birth, Elsa was given her father's surname, using the feminine form "Zelenskaya." But she is now believed to have dropped the inconvenient name in favor of her mother's Tikhonova, according to the Daily Mail .
Tikhonova's older sister Maria Vorontsova, 41, is Putin's first daughter from his marriage to ex-wife Lyudmila Ocheretnaya, 68. Vorontsova has two children, ages 14 and 9.
Putin's rumored longtime lover Alina Kabaeva, 43, is only a few years older than both of his daughters. She reportedly has four children with the dictator, including two sons called Ivan and Vladimir.

articles.title_orig: Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts and their impact topping the agenda
articles.title_zh: Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts and their impact topping the agenda
articles.content_orig:
MANILA, Philippines — Southeast Asian leaders opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila on Sunday for three days of talks, including dialogues with world leaders led by U.S. President Donald Trump, whose crucial trip to Asia could help boost his standing after his party’s defeat in the midterm elections.
The talks by the leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their expanded discussions with Asian and Western heads of state would focus on the world’s most troubling conflicts led by the war in the Middle East, according to drafts of post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press.
Trump is expected to land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. turns over the regional bloc’s rotating annual leadership to Singapore, Philippine officials said.
The ASEAN leaders are likely to renew calls for self-restraint and peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including longstanding disputes in the South China Sea and a civil war in Myanmar. They are also expected to press efforts to shield their economies and citizens from continuing fallout from intractable global conflicts.
“We reaffirmed our shared commitment to upholding international law, including the United Nations Charter,” the leaders’ draft statement says.
The statement also underlines the “importance of the peaceful resolution of disputes, upholding freedom of navigation and overflight and other lawful uses of the sea, including the right of transit passage in straits used for international navigation.”
Marcos said it’s crucial that despite the 11-nation regional bloc’s diversity, it has remained committed to remaining united in the face of headwinds.
“That commitment matters even more as the waters around us turn on shifting tides, geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, new technologies, climate change and transnational threats,” Marcos said in his opening remarks before ASEAN counterparts in a heavily secured convention center by Manila Bay.
Marcos warned problems across the world “are reshaping our region faster than any one country can respond to alone.”
But unity has been an elusive objective in ASEAN, a diverse bloc of democracies and authoritarian states, many of which are aligned with the United States or China.
ASEAN is known more for photo-ops projecting unity, cultural pomp and pageantry than for effectively dealing with the region’s conflicts, including Myanmar and the South China Sea.
Trump will join three key meetings late Tuesday, including a meeting of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue consisting of the United States, Japan, Australia and India, a grouping largely seen as a counterweight to China. He also will take part in a special summit with ASEAN leaders over cocktails, according to Philippine officials.
Trump will meet Wednesday with Marcos, who will receive him with a red-carpet welcome and a state luncheon at Manila’s presidential palace. They are expected to renew a commitment to their countries’ decades-old treaty alliance before flying separately to Shenzhen city in China for the APEC summit hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“The short stop in Manila will help reassure allies and partners that they aren’t being forgotten before he jets off to Shenzhen to focus on meetings with Xi,” U.S.-based geopolitical analyst Greg Poling said.
He added that the midterm electoral setback suffered by Republicans will hound Trump in Asia.
“In China, the administration has been trying to lower expectations; there will be no substantive progress made between Trump and Xi,” Poling said. “With Trump politically weakened after the midterm drubbing here, it is likely that the Chinese side will be even less interested in making any compromises.”
China will be represented in the Manila summit by its premier, Li Qiang, who will meet ASEAN leaders on Monday but leave before Trump arrives, Philippine officials said.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang's daughter was on the rise inside Nvidia. Succession may have come too soon.
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang's daughter was on the rise inside Nvidia. Succession may have come too soon.
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia caps a tumultuous week for the chipmaker, with his resignation coming less than a week after his extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy became public.
But the seeds for Huang's downfall were planted much earlier. The woman with whom he had a relationship, Alice Huang (no relation), arrived on the tech scene in 2023, when she became the managing director of Singapore-based data center Megaspeed International .
Megaspeed, which says it has complied with U.S. laws, would proceed to buy billions of dollars in Nvidia chips and servers. Over the past two years, Alice Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, has been photographed and recorded socializing with Jensen Huang, prompting questions in May from one quizzical investor about their "uncomfortably close relationship."
In a statement on Sunday, Nov. 15, Megaspeed said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025, and it denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business." "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.
Below is a timeline of events that led to Jensen Huang's startling resignation:
Alice Huang, a former television reporter in China, joins investment firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Management as deputy general manager, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database. Shanghai Hexi was founded by Kang Wei, who became her husband, according to the Wall Street Journal.
7Road International, originally incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, is renamed Megaspeed, and ownership of the "neocloud" company is transferred to Huang Le Ltd., an enterprise controlled by Alice Huang. She becomes its managing director.
Cloud-computing company Shanghai Century Litong is founded. A company linked to Alice's sister, Huang Yu, held an ownership stake.
Nvidia designates Shanghai Century Litong as a preferred cloud partner, giving the Chinese company priority access to Nvidia's chips, according to The Information .
Megaspeed's shares were transferred to another Singapore company, Swiftdata, and Alice Huang ceased to be listed as a director of the company, according to news site Caixin Global.
Information technology firm NetThunder posted a picture on social media of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang with other tech executives at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan.
Megaspeed's assets exploded from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, according to financial filings reviewed by Reuters.
Shipment records from December 2024 through early 2026, analyzed by short-selling firm Culper Research, suggest that Megaspeed's Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, imported about $4 billion in products from a company that builds equipment with Nvidia chips.
Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, jointly pitched Chinese investors on a Southeast Asia data center project, reportedly telling them they had "no problem securing GPUs" — the graphics processing units Nvidia specializes in — and citing Alibaba as a customer, according to the Financial Times.
Jensen Huang meets with President Trump at the White House. It marks their first of many White House encounters in Mr. Trump's second term.
Singapore opens an investigation into Megaspeed and several other companies over suspected false declarations related to the purchase of servers and other offenses, according to Bloomberg News.
Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are recorded on video together at a dinner at San Liu Shi Fu restaurant in Taipei, around the time of the Computex tech conference in Taiwan.
Jensen Huang says the technology giant has won approval from the Trump administration to sell its advanced H20 computer chips, used to develop artificial intelligence, to China, a reversal of prior administration policy.
"It's so innovative and dynamic here in China that it's really important that American companies are able to compete and serve the market here in China," Huang said at the time.
That same month, Nvidia becomes the first public company to be worth $4 trillion.
Chinese police detained Kang Wei, Alice Huang's husband and business partner, in connection with suspected stock manipulation, sources told Caixin.
That same month, Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country after she downplayed her role at Megaspeed amid the country's investigation into its operations, according to a Bloomberg News report.
Jensen Huang boards Air Force One in Alaska to accompany Mr. Trump on a two-day trip to Beijing.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Mr. Trump about the counterintelligence risk posed by Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The briefing, which occurred before Jensen Huang joined the trip, was the second briefing Mr. Trump had received from U.S. intelligence about the Nvidia CEO's relationship, the Times reported.
Jensen Huang attends Mr. Trump's state dinner for China's Xi Jinping at the White House.
Jensen Huang attends an AI event at the White House and signs a set of voluntary AI safety standards amid calls for tighter guardrails on the technology.
Jensen Huang writes a message to Nvidia employees admitting that he had an extramarital affair. The same day, Nvidia's board said it had launched an independent investigation amid reports that its CEO was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
The New York Times on Nov. 8 reported that U.S. government surveillance suggested Alice Huang was feeding information directly to Beijing.
At an impromptu press conference at the White House, Mr. Trump said he had spoken to Jensen Huang and that the tech exec had indicated he was unaware of Alice Huang's links to China's intelligence services. Mr. Trump also described the Nvidia CEO as an "honorable man" who's "definitely suffering."
Mr. Trump didn't address questions about when he first learned about the spy allegations, only saying, "not too long ago" and that "it didn't make much of an impact on me."
The New York Times reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, a subordinate at Nvidia.
Nvidia's board of directors announces that Jensen Huang has resigned, effective immediately.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: US, China, Russia plan unprecedented meeting at APEC
articles.title_zh: US, China, Russia plan unprecedented meeting at APEC
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO J ensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.
Officials also said that Elon Musk , the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.
The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.
"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."
Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."
"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.
Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."
China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.
Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed , a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.
The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.
During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.
"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.
"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."

articles.title_zh: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe into reports about its business
articles.content_orig:
Megaspeed told CNBC Sunday that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and said it has launched an internal probe into media reports concerning its business and supply chain.
The Singapore-based cloud computing company has faced heightened scrutiny since former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife following reports linking him to former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times.
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Nov. 12 amid fallout from reports about his extramarital relationships, one of which was reportedly a direct report.
"Ms. Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the Company," Megaspeed said in an emailed statement shared with CNBC. "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," it added.
Megaspeed describes itself as a "core business partner" of Nvidia's computing power cloud business in the region, allowing customers to rent computing power from Nvidia GPUs, or graphics processing units — specialized chips designed to do many calculations at the same time.
The company, which has offices in Singapore and Indonesia, has previously faced media and government scrutiny over whether chips supplied through its business were redirected to customers in China.
Megaspeed said Sunday that media reports about its business, supply chain and global operations are not supported by verifiable evidence and it has retained external legal counsel to conduct a "thorough internal investigation."
"Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," it said.
The company added that it will review the reporting and communicate further with stakeholders as appropriate.
— CNBC's Anniek Bao and Jenni Reid helped contribute to this report.

“Air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia towards Riyadh,” Turki al-Maliki, the Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, said in a post on X early on Sunday.
He said the coalition forces also shot down three drones in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern region on Sunday.
Earlier on Saturday, al-Maliki said two suspected Houthi drones “were intercepted and destroyed” in the Riyadh and southern regions.
Meanwhile, the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), claimed to have shot down an armed Saudi coalition reconnaissance aircraft carrying out “hostile operations in the airspace of al-Jawf”.
In a post on X, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Iran-aligned group was able to “repel a number of Saudi military formations using several Yemeni-made surface-to-air missiles” and that it was the fifth aircraft the Houthis had shot down since the escalation began.
At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to the kingdom’s authorities.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport, as well as the East-West pipeline and oil infrastructure in eastern and southern Saudi Arabia.
The interceptions come as the Saudi-led forces supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government also said they intercepted several drones launched towards the Yemeni city of Marib.
Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili said government forces had made gains against the Houthis during heavy fighting in the al-Hazm and Madghal districts of al-Jawf, as fighting intensified in Marib.
Al-Nuzaili said 321 Houthi leaders had been killed or wounded in 723 targeted operations by Saudi-backed forces in the Taiz, Lahij, Marib and al-Jawf governorates, and that 117 military vehicles used by the Iran-allied rebel group had been destroyed.
The coalition carried out at least 37 air strikes and 56 drone attacks, as well as 541 artillery strikes.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the Saudi-led coalition had launched 72 air strikes against the Houthis in the Saada, Taiz, Lahij and al-Jawf governorates over the past 24 hours.
He said the Houthis targeted Yemen’s Saudi-backed forces in the Kharaz area of the Lahij governorate with ballistic missiles.
Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported that two women and two children were injured as a result of artillery shelling by Saudi-backed forces in a residential neighbourhood of the Shuaub district in Sanaa, Yemen’s capital controlled by the Houthis.
More than 340,000 people have been displaced as a result of fighting in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration.
As the fight between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis escalated, the US Embassy in Riyadh issued a nationwide security alert on Saturday urging Americans in the kingdom to exercise “heightened vigilance”, citing an increased threat of Houthi attacks.
The embassy said Houthi attacks on airports and other critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia had “caused civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions”, warning that hostilities could spread “rapidly”.
“Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia,” it said.

articles.title_orig: Study Hard, Get a Career and Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
articles.title_zh: Study Hard, Get a Career and Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
articles.content_orig:
Protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself.
In India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious.
In France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting.
In both countries, the anger of the students shows no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain.
It is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement.
The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” said Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?”

articles.title_orig: US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
US envoy Jared Kushner has said he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to advance peace talks to the next stage, including facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Moscow.
Kushner told reporters on Saturday that “both sides” – Kyiv and Moscow – know that compromises will be necessary to end Russia’s war on Ukraine, and that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were now working on the next steps.
US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law’s comments follow peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday that failed to reach a breakthrough on ending the war, but resulted in a prisoner exchange .
The prospect of Europe’s involvement in the talks has grown in recent weeks, with leaders agreeing on Friday to send five representatives of European countries to represent the bloc at future peace talks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he did not believe it was possible to think about European security “without Europe”.
The Kremlin has signalled openness to negotiations with Europe, but has criticised a lack of proposals from the bloc.
The five countries attending – France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom – have signalled a readiness to send troops as part of a “coalition of the willing” to secure Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire.
Al Jazeera’s Mike Hanna, reporting from Washington, DC, said that the Russian “acceptance, as it has been accepted by Jared Kushner of European participation [in the talks], is something that could actually be important”.
“Kushner makes direct reference as well to the issue of security guarantees required by Ukraine, and he makes clear that it would be NATO that would provide these guarantees,” Hanna said.
Moreover, he added, “as negotiators are suggesting, there might be another round of multilateral negotiations to build on what’s been called ‘substantial progress’ in the recent talks”.
In a lengthy post on X on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron said Europe must “state clearly” what it wants for the post-war period, “including to the Russians”.
Macron also stated his belief that Ukraine, which has Europe’s largest conventional army, has a key role to play in Europe’s post-war context alongside NATO, which he added is a “place where it fully belongs”.
Zelenskyy said on Friday that US negotiators had asked during the Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from its eastern region of Donbas, most of which Russia occupies, in exchange for joining NATO.
The war has raged while negotiations continue. November leaks from Russia’s official statistics agency showed that Moscow’s war effort has so far cost the lives of at least 450,000 soldiers.

articles.title_orig: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
articles.title_zh: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
articles.content_orig:
Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings
The global political centre of gravity will be firmly in Asia this week as world leaders fly in for back-to-back high-level summits against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.
Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections .
The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy .
Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.
Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy.
“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.”
Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines , starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend.
While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia.
Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea , where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region.
The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec.
For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”.
The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers.
Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner.
Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU.
“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum.
Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea.
China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters.
Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas . Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term.
A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore .
Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration . Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative.
Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo speaks of community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes town
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo speaks of community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes town
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has spoken about the "suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future", which he said had left communities under threat, during a visit to an isolated Andean village in his former diocese.
About 6,000 people live in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, located in a remote part of the Andes mountains of northern Peru, but the Pope's visit still drew a crowd of about 20,000, according to the Vatican.
At an outdoor Mass, the Pope spoke of "declining birth rates that are emptying villages" and the unequal distribution of the land's resources.
More than 40% of the population in the Cajamarca region, where the town is located, live in poverty - the highest figure in Peru, according to official data.
Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru.
In his sermon, the Pope thanked those who had made the journey to see him and emphasised the importance of never losing heart, despite life's difficulties.
The pontiff's Latin America tour comes roughly a month after he underwent surgery to remove part of his right lung after a cancerous lump was found during routine checks.
At the start of his trip, he said the care he had received made him think of those who "lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment for health conditions.
Santa Cruz is within the Diocese of Chiclayo, where the Pope served as bishop from 2015 to 2023. During his tenure, he visited Santa Cruz several times a year to minister to the town's rural population.
On Saturday, he returned by helicopter and was greeted by singing and cheering. He later did a tour in a popemobile, from which he waved to people who had travelled to see him.
Speaking at a local parish on Saturday, the 71-year-old said he felt "joy" at being able to visit the small town once again.
"It is like a very big dream that the Lord has allowed this servant to come here," he said.
Rev Kevin Noriega, who was ordained in 2018 by the then-bishop, told Reuters the visit had brought "enormous hope and emotion" to Santa Cruz.
He said: "People are eager to experience this Holy Mass ... because after so much time they will be able to see their bishop - 'Father Robert', as they used to call him - now as the Holy Father."
Peru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the leader of the Catholic church, who was elected in May 2025.
The 12-day trip has included stops in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in Peru carries personal significance.
The US-born Pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.
The pontiff is set to leave Chiclayo on Sunday, when he will head to Cusco and then on to a Peruvian section of the Amazon rainforest. His tour of the region will conclude on Monday, at which point he will return to Rome.

articles.title_zh: Italy fines Meta $887m for accessing Android users’ photos and videos
articles.content_orig:
Italian regulators fined Facebook parent company Meta $880 million for accessing users' photos without their "specific" consent, the country's data protection authority said on Saturday.
Through the Facebook application for Android devices, Meta accessed photographs, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users "without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them," the authority said in a statement.
Saturday's latest fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant. In 2021, Amazon received a more than 1.1 billion euro, or about $1.2 billion, fine for breaching competition law.
That sum was subsequently reduced to 752 million euros, or about $829 million, on appeal.
Meta may also appeal the latest fine. The tech company had not responded to a request for comment by Saturday afternoon.
Meta has been fined or ordered to pay settlements over privacy issues. In September, a judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25 billion to the state after a jury found that the social media company deceived consumers for years about its data privacy policies. The company said they disagreed with the jury's verdict.

articles.content_orig:
Howard Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology to Asia, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales in the region. Credit... Doug Mills/The New York Times
By Ana Swanson Tripp Mickle Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan
Ana Swanson, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported from Washington, and Tripp Mickle from San Francisco.
There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.
Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.
The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang , was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company , sending the company’s shares tumbling.
The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.
The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.
Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

Donald Trump will meet Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China next week for an unprecedented three-way meeting between the leaders of the US , Russia , and China, with nuclear weapons and the war in Iran expected to be on the agenda.
The meeting will take place on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, the White House confirmed on Friday. It will bring together the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers for the first time, although all three have held bilateral talks with one another.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The meeting comes nine months after the expiry of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), the last major nuclear arms control agreement between Washington and Moscow.
The treaty, which expired in February, had placed limits on the two countries’ strategic nuclear arsenals, leaving the world’s two largest nuclear powers without those restrictions for the first time in more than half a century.
Mr Trump has rejected Russia's offer to extend it for another year, saying he wanted a new agreement that would also include China.
Beijing has resisted joining such negotiations, arguing that its nuclear arsenal is much smaller than those of Washington and Moscow. China has more than 600 nuclear warheads, compared with more than 5,000 each for Russia and the US.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told reporters, according to Reuters. “This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think ​it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have ​adult conversations about adult things.”
Mr Trump also intends to discuss the war in Iran with Mr Xi and Mr Putin, but Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is not expected to feature, the official said. “We’ve had many meetings ⁠recently with ​the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, ​so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official said.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly insisted that his country must be involved in any discussions about its future.
Russia had previously proposed the three-way meeting, with Mr Putin reportedly keen to use it to discuss Ukraine. The Russian president had floated the idea during a telephone conversation with Trump last month, according to the Wall Street Journal .
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha had warned against giving Putin such a platform. “Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandisement and give him a stature he does not deserve,” he said last month, adding that it would only “encourage Putin to continue this war”.
The planned summit has also drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain, and the Soviet Union discussed the postwar settlement in Europe. The prospect of Mr Trump, Mr Putin, and Mr Xi meeting without Ukraine has revived concerns about major powers making decisions that affect other countries without consulting them.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the comparison, saying that any agreements reached in Shenzhen could not be imposed on other countries. He nevertheless described a meeting between the three leaders as “extremely significant”. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect,” he said.
Mr Trump is due to visit Manila on Tuesday for talks with leaders of the Association of South-east Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen. He is also scheduled to hold bilateral talks and a working lunch with Xi on Thursday, ahead of the trilateral meeting.
The White House said billionaire Elon Musk would accompany Mr Trump on the China visit, but a senior US official said he would not attend the talks with Mr Xi and Mr Putin.

articles.title_orig: US aviation shutdown blamed on L3 Harris installed router
articles.title_zh: US aviation shutdown blamed on L3 Harris installed router
articles.content_orig:
Airlines canceled thousands more flights Saturday as they recovered from Friday's nationwide ground stop, but the FAA said schedules should be back to normal by the end of Sunday.
More than 5,000 U.S. flights had been canceled Saturday as of 2:48 p.m. ET, according to FlightAware , already past the top of the 4,000 to 5,000 that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford predicted. Flight-tracking app Flighty said the outage has now caused more cancellations than the 2024 CrowdStrike software failure. "I do think the worst is behind us," Bedford said, and he apologized to travelers.
The FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours Friday, the longest ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. About 12,000 flights couldn't be completed, Bedford said.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the outage began while L3Harris Technologies, which runs the network, was doing routine work to switch lines from copper wire to fiber at a remote FAA site. A router involved in the work flooded the rest of the system, disrupting communications with airplanes and radar. Duffy said officials are working to determine "whether we had incompetence" by the contractor or a faulty router. "Until I can build" a new network, he said, "I'm stuck with L3Harris." Bedford said the review will determine whether the router was installed or configured incorrectly, or was simply defective.
In a statement to Yahoo News, L3Harris said it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation" and "takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." The company did not address Duffy's criticism or say what went wrong.
Asked why the work was done on a Friday afternoon, Duffy said work at small, remote sites is done during the day because it isn't expected to affect the wider system. "There'll be a reevaluation of when we do this work," he said. Bedford said maintenance on the network is logged on paper, so officials had to search through paper records to figure out who was working where.
Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, told Yahoo News that communications with some planes were disrupted during the outage and that controllers moved flights to working frequencies. Asked whether work like Friday's should be done during the day, he said, "If the worst outcome is we lose all of our frequencies, well, then that work should be done when there's the fewest airplanes in the sky."
The network's problems aren't new. A 2023 FAA-commissioned safety review called it obsolete, CBS News reported . In 2009, a technician for L3Harris' predecessor, Harris Corp., misconfigured a router while moving the network to fiber, disrupting 129 air traffic facilities, according to a Transportation Department inspector general review .
Duffy is pressing Congress for more money to replace the system. President Trump has asked for $30 billion and Duffy has said he wants $50 billion, on top of the $12.5 billion Congress approved last year. Bedford said the router swap was routine maintenance, not part of that modernization effort.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called on Duffy to resign Saturday. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, a Democrat from Illinois and a ranking member of an aviation subcommittee, called for an investigation .
Travelers whose flights were canceled are owed a refund if they choose not to fly, and most major airlines are offering travel waivers. Airlines' promises of hotels and meals generally cover only disruptions within their control, which doesn't include an FAA ground stop.
National Air Traffic Controllers Association President Nick Daniels speaks during a news conference at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on September 28, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
The head of the air traffic controllers' union told Yahoo News in a phone interview Saturday that communications with some planes were disrupted during Friday's outage. Controllers across the country had to scramble to keep flights moving safely, he said.
"We had controllers working with one another across the United States to see whose frequencies were working, whose radar was working," said Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association. Controllers checked whether they could hand off planes to one another if their own frequencies went down, he said.
Daniels said he hadn't reviewed the FAA's safety data. But asked what controllers had told him, he said, "We know we didn't have communications with airplanes, or that we were switching airplanes to different frequencies because their communications were being disrupted." Controllers "ensured the safety of every aircraft," he said.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a news conference earlier Saturday that "no facilities went dark," but acknowledged reports of "certain frequencies that were going in and out."
Asked whether work like Friday's should be done during the day, Daniels said it depends on the risk. "If the worst outcome is we lose all of our frequencies, well, then that work should be done when there's the fewest airplanes in the sky," he said. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that work at small, remote sites is routinely done during the day and that the practice will be reevaluated.
Daniels said such failures often happen when the FAA's required safety reviews before maintenance aren't followed. He said he didn't know whether that happened Friday.
Daniels wouldn't say whether Duffy was right to blame contractor L3Harris. "I don't think blame changes anything. Action changes things," Daniels said. He said the union has warned for more than a decade that the system is failing, noting that the FAA still uses floppy disks in some cases to update computers.
Daniels said any new money for the air traffic control system should also go toward controllers' pay and working conditions. He said he hasn't spoken with Duffy since the outage, but that Duffy "already knows" the union's position. "We're going to continue working on that with this administration," he said.
More than 5,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. had been canceled Saturday as of 2:48 p.m. ET, according to FlightAware . FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had predicted 4,000 to 5,000 cancellations for the day.
American has canceled the most flights, 892, followed by Delta (734), United (733) and Southwest (540). JetBlue has canceled 43% of its schedule.
The air traffic control system itself appears to be running near normal, and no airports had ground stops in effect Saturday afternoon. The problem now is getting planes and crews back where they're supposed to be.
Sunday looks better so far. About 130 U.S. flights scheduled for Sunday had been canceled as of Saturday afternoon.
L3Harris Technologies said Saturday it is supporting the FAA's investigation into Friday's outage. Earlier that day, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy publicly questioned whether the company's "incompetence" caused the outage.
"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," an L3Harris spokesperson said in a statement to Yahoo News. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."
The company said that, "together with its telco partners and the FAA," it has completed more than 70% of the planned switch from copper wire to fiber optic lines. The statement doesn't say what caused the outage or respond to Duffy's suggestion of contractor error.
Asked whether L3Harris employees or a partner company did Friday's work, and whether the company disputes Duffy's suggestion of contractor error, a spokesperson said the company had nothing to offer beyond its statement.
Airlines' biggest challenge Saturday is getting pilots and flight attendants to the planes they're scheduled to fly.

articles.title_orig: What Travelers Caught in the Air-Travel Delays Need to Know
articles.title_zh: What Travelers Caught in the Air-Travel Delays Need to Know
articles.content_orig:
"The airlines are trying to get back to normal."
As air travel in the United States remains hectic due to the lingering effects from Friday's ground stop , a travel expert said preparation and patience are key for flyers who are trying to reach their destination.
Brett Snyder, the president of the travel planning service Cranky Concierge, said that flight schedules will likely not be back to normal until Monday at the earliest as airlines scramble to get their fleets and crews back to their planned destinations as orderly as possible.
A total of over 14,000 flights were canceled Friday and Saturday, according to FlightAware. Around 160 flights on Sunday have been canceled as of Saturday afternoon, FlightAware said.
The FAA said the ground stop was instituted due to a telecommunications issue in the air traffic control system.
FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the system is expected to be fully recovered by Sunday.
"The point of the cancellations and delays today is to right the ship as quick as possible and by Monday everything is as smooth as possible," Snyder told ABC News Saturday.
Snyder said that while there's not a lot passengers can do while the airlines and airports recover, there are key steps they can take to help ensure their flights go as smooth as possible.
The first thing that flyers should consider is if it's worth waiting for their flight if it has been delayed or if they should rebook, he said.
"If this was a trip that was going to be short and fun and not a big deal, I'd scrap it," Snyder said.
Snyder said that most airlines are offering refunds during this situation, even if their planned flight is delayed.
American Airlines announced Saturday it is adding fare caps across their domestic and short international flights as delays are expected to continue. American, Southwest, Delta and United are all offering travelers waivers.
Travelers are entitled to refunds for flights canceled by the airlines, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation.
"The consumer is entitled to a refund if the airline cancelled a flight, regardless of the reason, and the consumer chooses not to travel or accept travel credits, vouchers, or other forms of compensation offered by the airline," DOT says on its website .
Additionally, travelers are entitled to a refund if a flight is significantly delayed or changed and they choose not to accept credits, vouchers or other compensation offered by the airline.
DOT defines a significantly delayed flight as three or more hours after the original scheduled arrival time for domestic flights.
For those who are still pushing ahead with their trip, Snyder said it's best to stay at the airport and remain on top of any updates. He recommended travelers download the airline's app and keeping an eye on all the alerts associated with their flight.
Snyder noted that flyers should pay close attention to any connecting flights and check if they are canceled. Airlines are typically good at rebooking customers during those situations, he added.
When in doubt, Snyder recommended that flyers call their airlines. If they are in the airport, talk to an agent, he said.
He stressed that ticket holders should remain courteous to the representatives.
"Remember the airline employees are going through this just as much you are as a traveler. Go easy on them, they're trying to help you," Snyder said.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters Saturday that the federal government is working around the clock to help the airlines and airports navigate through the issues and get service back to normal as fast as possible.
"You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most," Duffy said in a post on X earlier Saturday.
"Our top priority right now is making sure travelers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible," Duffy said.

The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop just after 8 p.m. on Friday
NEW YORK (WABC) -- Thousands of travelers across the New York area are grappling with the effects of a nationwide ground stop, with nearly 2,000 flights canceled across the country on Saturday.
The disruptions are being felt across the region at Newark Liberty International Airport, John F. Kennedy International Airport, and LaGuardia Airport, as passengers face delays, cancellations, and uncertain travel plans. Officials are hoping operations return to normal before the busy Thanksgiving travel period begins.
Port Authority released a statement Saturday saying,
"Travelers should anticipate continued delays and cancellations at the region's airports throughout the weekend as airlines recover from Friday night's nationwide FAA ground stop. By the end of Friday evening, JFK, LaGuardia, and New York Stewart airports had reported more than 800 cancellations and more than 600 delays.
Airlines are continuing to work through the logistical challenges created by Friday's disruption. Planes were left out of position across the country, and some flight attendants reached their allowable duty limits, requiring carriers to reassign crews and equipment before flights can return to normal schedules.
15% of flights were canceled out of Newark Saturday, 21% at LaGuardia, and 21% at JFK Airport. There were dozens of delays at all three airports.
On Friday evening at LaGuardia, one of the nation's busiest transportation hubs, only a handful of international flights were arriving after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered all flights to stop departing.
Video from the airport around 4:30 p.m. showed aircraft on the runway. About 30 minutes later, roughly a dozen planes were stopped in place as pilots received instructions to return to their gates.
"Nobody is allowed to leave the ground. If you are on the ground, please return to the gate immediately," pilots were told.
Even after flights resumed, some travelers remained stranded or scrambling to adjust their plans.
One passenger trying to reach Belize said the disruption left him frustrated after he missed his flight.
"Unfortunately, we did not make over our flight ... hopefully make it home," he said.
The FAA said it issued the nationwide ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."
Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a press conference Saturday.
"We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related. So we want to be clear that we have a equipment issue, and we're working through what this defective piece of equipment was," Bedford said.
"When we have that root cause analysis complete, we'll share it with you," Bedford said.
He predicted the air travel schedule would fully recover by Sunday.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA does not believe the failure in communications that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday was the result of a cyber attack.
"In at least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire, and they were bringing it over to fiber," Duffy said during a press conference Saturday.
Duffy said this transfer from copper to fiber has been happening in the U.S. for decades, saying virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fiber, from analog to digital.
"Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment, that router that was being replaced as we switched from from copper to fiber, it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system. So specifically, we had over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, and what that did was gave us issues with our our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar feeds," Duffy said.
When that happened the airspace was shut down for safety, Duffy said.
"Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online, so we don't believe this was cyber at all. This was an FAA system that didn't meet, didn't meet the moment," Duffy said.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul released a statement saying: "America's airspace ground to a halt yesterday, leaving thousands of flights canceled and travelers stranded across the country. More than 3,500 planes were already in the air as radar and communications systems faltered. We're fortunate no lives were lost.
"From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system have become a pattern on Sean Duffy's watch.
"Through it all, he's been more focused on starring in his own reality show than addressing the crisis at his agency.
"With millions of Americans preparing to travel for the holidays, families deserve answers and confidence in the safety of our skies. Congress must launch a full investigation to determine what went wrong and ensure it never happens again.
"Sean Duffy must resign, or President Trump must remove him immediately."
Major airlines have issued travel waivers for affected passengers this weekend.
American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines are waiving change fees through Saturday, with United also waiving fare differences. Southwest Airlines is allowing passengers to rebook at no additional cost through Monday.
Travelers are encouraged to check directly with their airline and review the status of their itinerary before heading to the airport as carriers continue working to minimize delays and cancellations.
The disruption marked the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned.
Before that, the last nationwide ground stop occurred after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.
